fieldMarks: Raised scales over the eyes look like horns (NDOW; NPS Death Valley).
Heavy-bodied pit viper, tan to lighter cream with dark dorsal blotches; large triangular head (NDOW; NPS Death Valley).
Usually 1.5 ft or less, up to about 3 ft; 17-33 in (NPS Death Valley; NDOW).
Moves by throwing the body sideways in an S-shaped curve; tracks in sand are J-shaped and may end in a small depression where it has buried itself (NPS Death Valley).
behavior: Crepuscular, and nocturnal in warm periods; by day it hides in rodent burrows or shifts side to side until nearly buried in sand, then waits for prey (NPS Death Valley).

Active mainly February-November in extreme southern California; in the eastern Mojave Desert activity starts March or April and ends October or November, peaking May-June and late September-October (NatureServe).
Eats mainly lizards, pocket mice, kangaroo rats and other small mammals; occasionally small birds and snakes (NatureServe).
Seasonal moves of up to several hundred metres between hibernation burrows and sandy summer habitat were recorded in the eastern Mojave (NatureServe).
habitat: Open desert with fine windblown sand, sandy washes, or sparsely vegetated dunes with creosotebush or mesquite; sometimes rocky or gravelly sites (NatureServe).
Overwinters in rodent or tortoise burrows (NatureServe).
range: Southeastern California, southern Nevada and extreme southwestern Utah south through southwestern Arizona into northeastern Baja California and northwestern Sonora; from below sea level to about 1,830 m (NatureServe).
